newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH CROWN IN FOR FURTHER BATTLE, BUT SHOULD WIN.
newsitem.headline: CZECH CROWN IN FOR FURTHER BATTLE, BUT SHOULD WIN.

text.p: Downward pressure on the Czech crown has subsided following a series of Czech National Bank (CNB) moves, but analysts warned on Tuesday that another attack on the currency is likely as the CNB measures are eased.

After months of rock-solid stability, the crown came under fire last week from short-selling that pushed it to record lows of below the five percent level of its basket parity, prompting the CNB to intervene for the first time in more than a year.
The CNB said the crown's fall was due to fluctuations of several foreign currencies and not for fundamental reasons, adding that the bearish pressure has subsided this week.
But analysts said that no matter what the reason was for the first attempt, they expect another attack to try to drive the crown down to begin once the central bank begins to loosen its grip.
"What tends to happen in situations like this is that you get a second attack...and I think you have to expect that," said Pavel Pinkava, a London-based currency dealer at Nomura International.

Added Pavel Sobisek of Zivnostenska Banka in Prague: "The CNB showed a strong committment to keep the crown at current levels. (But) similar attacks (on the crown) look quite probable for the future."

In an attempt to ward off bearish investors, the central bank raised its Lombard rate to 50 percent from a previous 14 percent, and followed up with a rise in repo rates to 45 percent from 12.9 percent.

The moves, which analysts say may have cost the central bank as much as $1 billion, appeared to have had their desired effect with banks raising rates and the crown steadying at about 2.0 percent below parity of the central bank's mark/dollar basket in Tuesday afternoon trading from -3.8 percent on Friday.
Analysts said that if the central bank continues to stand its ground, it should be able to win the war and beat back the tide of weaker crown sentiment.
"The CNB has got to stand tough right now. It is under government pressure over the economy but if it holds on, it can withstand another wave and win this battle," said one local dealer.

"Over the next couple of weeks, the market will be pretty quiet, and then there will be a final attack, which I think will resolve itself in favour of the central bank, and then they (investors) will walk away," he added.

Nomura's Pinkava agreed saying that the central bank will have to hold rates at current levels for two to three weeks, but that in the end, as is often the case, the central bank should come out on top.

"At the end of the day, these crises often resolve themselves in favour of the central bank, especially the first few times investors attack and especially in this market which isn't that deep," he said.
